newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - UK-Florida air cargo rivalry hits yields.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - UK-Florida air cargo rivalry hits yields.

text.p: Viking Freight Services, a British air cargo space selling company, flew 4,500 tonnes during its first nine months of trading -- February-October 1996 -- when it earned revenues totalling 2.5 million stg, said managing director Kevin Durnin.

The company is contracted by Unijet to sell freight capacity on the British tour operator's Leisure International Airways flights and has a similar agreement to book cargo on Monarch Airlines McDonnell Douglas DC-10 holiday charter flights from Britain, Durnin said.

"It has been a very tough first year because of the huge amount of aircraft capacity that was available on our main routes, from Britain to Florida, during the summer. Therefore, I am very pleased with our performance," he noted.

"Because of all the cargo space made available by the likes of Virgin, Britannia Airways, Airtours, a rejuvenated Delta Air Lines and the former Excalibur Airways,I estimate year-on-year yields between Britain and the south-east U.S. quadrant from Houston to Charlotte (North Carolina) were down by 15 percent in summer 1996," he said.

He added that during the peak period, some 84 wide-body flights were being operated each week between the UK and Florida. "That's 12 flights a day -- about the same frequency as that on the UK-New York route. It was inevitable that cargo yields took a hammering," said Durnin.

He said that in order to improve cargo yields on Leisure International's westbound 10-tonne capacity Boeing 767-300 and six-tonne capacity DC-10 flights from London Gatwick and Manchester to Orlando during the summer, he had tapped new areas in order to win more business.

"In particular, we trucked freight regularly from Florida all the way over to Los Angeles. It may sound a crazy policy but it worked because the California market was much less susceptible to downward rates pressure than the south-east U.S.," Durnin said.

He added that Viking Freight also signed tactical agreements with carriers such as Challenge Air, Fine Air, Tampa and Aeromexico, which flew cargo carried in by Leisure International from Britain onward from Miami down to Central and South America.
"So, westbound across the Atlantic, we managed to keep away from the worst of the rate wars. But eastbound, we had to drop our rates and competed head-to-head on price," he said.
Durnin said during the present winter season, Leisure International had reduced its Britain-Florida schedule from the summer average of 11 to five to six a week.

"Because of the off-peak season, a lot of the competition has disappeared and so our yields have improved. And this situation has been helped by the introduction of fuel surcharges. But while we will again be operating 11 flights a week, I don't know what other airlines will be doing come April 1997 and the start of the summer season," he said.

From November 1, Leisure International switched its Florida flights from Orlando to Sandford, 28 miles north of the city, where an airport specially designed to cater for tour operators has been established, he said.

Durnin added that Unijet's three weekly 767 package holiday flights to the Dominican Republic had attracted good return cargo loads of exotic fruit. But for cargo, other Caribbean points served had proved to be disappointing.
"As for expansion, Viking Freight is currently talking to a British and a U.S. airline about managing their freight products but it is too early to say any more," he said.
"We would love to sell cargo to other areas of the world and this was the original plan. But there are not as many opportunities available as I first thought," he said.
